items.text: Which division of authority should normally govern a country with national and regional governments?

options.label: Each level should have some powers that the other cannot take away unilaterally.
The national government may delegate regional powers and reclaim them when appropriate.
Regional governments should be able to reclaim any powers given to the national government.
The right arrangement depends on the issue and the country.

items.notes: Distinguishes a federal division from revocable national delegation and a confederation. Generic local preference does not suffice. This question is authored content, not a validated scale indicator.

items.text: A national government wants one uniform policy on a matter assigned by the constitution to regional governments. The regional policy protects rights equally well. What should settle the conflict?

options.label: The protected regional authority should stand unless the constitution is properly changed.
The national government should be able to override the region for uniformity.
Regional governments should control even matters assigned nationally.
Other features of the case would determine my view.

items.notes: Holds rights protection constant; checks whether decentralization is constitutionally protected rather than merely useful. This question is authored content, not a validated scale indicator.

items.text: Suppose breaking a well-justified rule in one case would clearly produce the best overall outcome, without weakening the rule for anyone else. What ultimately determines whether this act is right?

options.label: The consequences of this particular act.
Whether it follows a rule justified by the consequences of generally following it.
Whether it honors a duty that is not ultimately justified by consequences.
No single one of these always determines rightness.

items.notes: Act-outcome favors a narrow act-consequentialist criterion; rule-outcome favors rule consequentialism; rule-independent opposes both. This is about rightness, not the best everyday decision procedure. One answer is not independent corroboration. The act-outcome answer is a direct criterion in this specified case, not a complete utilitarian identity. Original authored wording has not been empirically tested.

items.text: What ultimately justifies a moral rule against harming an innocent person?

options.label: Following that rule generally produces better consequences than the alternatives.
A person's claim against being harmed can constrain us independently of the rule's overall consequences.
The rule is justified by principles affected people could reasonably accept.
More than one of these can justify the rule without any one being ultimate.

items.notes: General-consequences is a candidate rule-consequentialist ground. A person can endorse a useful rule without treating consequences as its ultimate justification. The agreement option is not automatically Scanlonian. This asks what ultimately justifies one kind of moral rule. Only the separate act-criterion question can establish whether a consequence-justified rule also determines this act’s rightness. Original wording has not been empirically tested.

items.text: Suppose someone weighs their reasons and chooses without pressure. The complete earlier state of the world and the laws of nature still fix that choice. Which view is closest to yours?

options.label: The choice cannot be genuinely free because it was fixed in that way.
The choice could still be genuinely free despite being fixed in that way.
Those facts alone do not settle whether this choice is genuinely free.

items.notes: Applied countercase for the free-will/determinism conditional. The third answer is nondirectional. No answer asserts that determinism is true, that people have free will, or that moral responsibility follows. Authored content; response processes and independence from AHI103 are untested.

items.text: A person has an experience that seems to them like a clear divine message about a factual matter. Before checking the claim independently, what weight should the experience itself have for that person?

options.label: It can give the person an initial factual reason in favor of the message, even if later evidence could defeat it.
It can prompt investigation, but by itself gives the person no factual reason to think the message is true.
That depends on further features of the experience or its context.

items.notes: Asks only whether the experience can supply a defeasible initial factual reason to its subject. The contextual answer is nondirectional. No answer says the message is true, confers outsider/public warrant, or has moral or legal authority. Authored content; response processes and independence from EPI032 are untested.

items.text: A stranger faces serious harm. You could prevent it at modest cost to yourself. Assume helping would not advance your own long-term good. What moral weight does the stranger's need have?

options.label: Their need gives me a duty to help.
Their need gives me a moral reason to help, but no duty.
Their need alone gives me no moral reason to help; only my own long-term good can do that.
The moral weight depends on further features of the situation.

items.notes: Authored contrast between an independent duty, a non-obligatory independent moral reason, and a reason arising only through the agent’s long-term good. Philosophical content reviewed for a narrow conjunction; respondent comprehension, localization, and empirical independence remain untested. No answer alone establishes the standard maximizing account of ethical egoism, a refusal to help, or Rand’s complete ethics.

items.text: Two explanations use different words, but no conceivable experience or action would differ if either were correct. After clarifying the words, which is closest to your view of their remaining disagreement?

options.label: There is no remaining substantive difference in what the explanations claim.
They may still make substantively different claims, even with no possible difference in experience or action.
The shared consequences are a reason to doubt the disagreement, but do not settle whether the claims differ.

items.notes: Original question about whether an apparently empty conceptual dispute remains substantive. The third option distinguishes treating consequences as useful from treating their absence as settling this specific conceptual dispute. It does not ask whether either explanation is true or identify a respondent as a pragmatist. Comprehension and independence from EPI103 are untested.

items.text: When comparing how good two outcomes are in themselves, apart from whether the action producing either is permitted, which is closest to your view?

options.label: Only how well affected beings fare ultimately makes an outcome better or worse; other features matter through their effects on well-being.
Well-being matters, but another feature can improve an outcome even when no being’s well-being changes.
Neither general claim fits; it depends on the kind of outcome.

items.notes: Revision 2 of the historical unreleased NEI124@1 draft removes a rights-priority option that could coexist with welfarist outcome value. This asks about outcome value, not whether a right constrains action. Original wording has not been comprehension-tested.

items.text: Imagine two otherwise identical worlds. In one, an uninhabited valley has striking natural beauty. Nobody will ever see it, and no living being is affected. Can that alone make this world better in itself?

options.label: Yes. Its beauty can make the world better even though no being benefits.
No. Without changing any being’s well-being, it does not make the world better.
I cannot tell from this case whether the world is better.

items.notes: A concrete independent-beauty counterexample. Rejecting this particular value is not enough to establish general welfarism; it must be read with NEI124@2. This is not a copy of a source thought experiment or a validated scale item.

items.text: For individual actions, the morally right option is the one that produces the greatest total well-being for everyone affected; a promise or other consideration matters to rightness only through its effects on well-being.
items.notes: A general statement of the total-well-being act criterion. Agreement alone is not interpreted; the separate promise case must point in the same direction. This is authored wording, not a validated item.

items.text: After making a valid promise to do A, you learn that doing B would produce greater total well-being for everyone affected, counting all effects of keeping or breaking the promise, including effects on trust. No other consequences differ. Which view best matches yours?

options.label: Doing B is the morally right choice: the act with greater total well-being is right.
Keeping the promise can be morally right even though it produces less total well-being.
The well-being difference matters, but it does not settle which act is right.
None of these fits my view.

items.notes: Revision 2 clarifies that the well-being comparison includes effects on trust and other consequences, addressing the unreleased NEI125@1 ambiguity. The promise answer opposes this scoped criterion; a welfare-is-a-reason-only answer is nondirectional. This is not a utilitarian identity item or validated scale.

items.text: Who should normally have effective control over major productive assets such as factories and large firms?

options.label: The workers who use them, through institutions they can genuinely govern.
The wider public, through institutions it can genuinely govern.
State officials, even if workers or the public have little control over decisions.
Private owners, within general rules protecting workers and others.
Different forms should coexist without one general default.
Another arrangement or a view not listed.

items.notes: Revision 2 adds a non-forced other response and source-linked targets. It asks about effective control over productive assets, not ownership title alone. Worker self-management and democratically accountable public control remain distinct options; neither settles markets or planning. PLI123@1 remains preserved in the unreleased draft.
